elements.text: Failure of Fine Air to exercise operational control over the cargo loading process
Failure of Aeromar to load the airplane as specified by Fine Air
Failure of the FAA to adequately monitor Fine Air’s operational control responsibilities for cargo loading
Failure of the FAA to ensure that known cargo-related deficiencies were corrected at Fine Air
Airplane misloaded to produce a more aft center of gravity
Incorrect stabilizer trim setting
Extreme pitch-up at rotation
Inadequate procedures for preparing and distributing cargo weight pallet distribution forms and final weight and balance load sheets
Security guard unaware of airplane change and instructed loaders based on incorrect form
Accident airplane initially loaded according to wrong load distribution (N30UA instead of N27UA)
Final load configuration did not match planned load for either airplane
Aeromar cargo loading supervisor failed to ensure pallets were loaded according to an approved load plan
Aeromar cargo loading supervisor failed to confirm that cargo was properly restrained
Fine Air failed to exercise adequate operational control of loading operations conducted by Aeromar
Fine Air's failure to exercise adequate operational control created an environment lacking verification of pallet weights and load distribution
Fine Air fostered a management philosophy allowing dispatch without verification and control procedures
Loaders were not aware of the potentially catastrophic consequences of misloading and failing to secure cargo
Miami Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) lacked clear management policies for sufficient surveillance
FSDO was not aggressive in its inspection and management of the Fine Air certificate
Broader failure of the FAA to adequately monitor air carriers, especially supplemental cargo carriers, with identified operational problems
National and regional aviation safety inspection programs not adequately identifying and addressing systemic safety problems
Insufficient FAA personnel and budget resources for adequate air carrier surveillance
Fine Air’s continuing analysis and surveillance program was not rigorous and failed to correct systemic maintenance deficiencies
Practice of logging significant maintenance discrepancies on return flights to Miami rather than immediately
Principal maintenance inspector and Fine Air management took no further action regarding logging discrepancies
Flightcrew properly certificated and qualified
No medical, behavioral, or physiological factors affected the flightcrew
Weather was not a factor
Airplane properly certificated, equipped, and maintained (except FDR)
No evidence of failures in airplane structures or flight control systems
Compressor surges caused by attitude before impact, not a factor in accident cause
Stall sequence made recovery unlikely
CG near or aft of limit
CG shift resulted in mistrimmed stabilizer
Mistrim presented pitch control problem
Mistrim required exceptional skills not expected of typical pilot
Training for flightcrews in dealing with misloading would improve recovery chances
No significant shift of cargo rearward at or before rotation
Difficult work environment has potential to cause loading errors
Formal training necessary for cargo handling personnel
Company procedures hindered flight engineer from checking pallet locks
Independent method for verifying weight and balance might have prevented accident
Cargo loading operations have direct effect on flight safety and should not be neglected by FAA
Permanent documentation of FDR readouts needed
Current inspection intervals for FDRs not adequate
FAA avionics inspectors may lack experience and training for FDR oversight
